summary:
Multi-speed Europe is the idea that EU countries can integrate at different speeds and levels. It matters because enlargement and political disagreements make it harder for all members to move together, and internal divisions can affect the EU’s actions abroad.

Differentiated participation already exists in areas such as the euro, Schengen and other shared policies. The idea gained prominence after the Cold War, when leaders sought to combine enlargement with deeper integration. Brexit and disagreements over Ukraine and Russia have renewed the debate.

In 2017, the European Commission set out possible paths for the EU, including allowing willing countries to cooperate more closely. In 2026, Germany proposed a leading group of six large economies to advance financial integration. Critics warned this could sideline smaller states. That year, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz proposed associate EU membership for Ukraine, with participation but no voting rights while reforms continue. These proposals reflect different routes to closer integration.
